content: One reasonable aim is to have Lean certification of a fully constructive build. A large fraction of practical systems use String. Interesting. I'll build my own limited String library for now. Looks like it's from String.toList
The axiom originates from docs#ByteArray.utf8DecodeChar?, but perhaps you should clarify on why you care about decoding unicode with constructive proofs that the unicode characters are valid.
(one such proof in question is here)

I do want constructive termination arguments. I want zero use of non-constructive axioms across my entire codebase (now of several 10's of KLOCs). None of it depends on mathlib. I was surprised to see a non-constructive axioms introduced by Lean core String.length.
Edited, this isn't about termination, but about validity of unicode characters
If you don't care about unicode at all, then you can juse use ByteArray instead of String

I want zero use of non-constructive axioms across my entire codebase

Can you elaborate on why?
Has nothing to do with Unicode characters. String.length drags a classical axiom into my otherwise entirely constructive project.
String is the type of sequences of unicode characters
Thanks, I think you're not understanding the issue.

String.length has to decode utf-8 to count the number of unicode code points, and has to prove that the resulting code point is legal. It is in this proof of legality that a classical axiom is being used

Kevin Sullivan said:

Has nothing to do with Unicode characters. String.length drags a classical axiom into my otherwise entirely constructive project.

Lean is not a good platform if you care about constructive reasoning. Neither the standard library nor any of the built-in tactics care about constructivism and will thus liberally pull in choice.
(though like Eric I would be curious about why this matters to you)
Ah, ok. Now is that a Lean implementation design/bootstrap issue, or something more fundamental.
It's a cultural thing, we don't care about constructivism.
And just using LEM or proof by contradiction makes things easier often times so proofs will just use them at will

It's maybe worth noting that a lot of people who claim to care about constructivism in Lean only really care about not being noncomputable (i.e. you can extract a C program from it), and of course Lean still cares a lot about String.length being computable!
FWIW https://github.com/zaz/cLEAN removes choice from String.toList
(specifically in https://github.com/zaz/cLEAN/commit/5d2fd56ccce8494ca15408251222643a43851692)

Thank you, all. Here's a related problem I had to work around, also with String.

Lean 's module system treats Lean-core defs whose bodies aren't `@[expose]d as opaque cross-module. (I'm wrong more than I'm right, so don't fear telling me if I'm wrong again.) At least Nat.toDigitsCore, Nat.toDigits, and Nat.digitChar are unexposed, so unfold, simp, and decide all get stuck on them.
import all lets you view the implementation of those opaque defs
Though usually they're opaque becaue you don't need to unfold them
Concerning choice, you may have a look at #35685, where I build my own version of Lean to limit the use of choice.
Hey, is lean4#13681 related to this thread or are there other reasons to dislike String.length? (e.g. utf8 reasons)
String.length is almost always not the function that you actually want for UTF-8 reasons.
The docstring says it measures in codepoints, sounds useful IMO, at least for end users even if it isn't useful for Lean itself. Is the plan to eliminate it entirely?

It gives you the count of utf-8 codepoints but this is neither the byte-size of the string nor the amount of user visible characters in the string. A codepoint is an abstract notion that has very little relation to what people actually perceive as a character in a modern string. In the future the plan is to remove String.length as a built-in function with O(1) guarantee. This has the crucial benefit that in our runtime we will be able to align the layout of ByteArray and String which will lead to less copying in IO-related applications. You will still be able to count the unicode codepoints by just taking the length of the character iterator (though now in O(n) as opposed to O(1)).

In particular, the majority of uses of String.length are wrong, for example using it to measure line length or using it to measure content length for visual alignment. Both of these are wrong if you are looking at a general UTF-8 string. If you believe you are looking at an ASCII only string you can just use utf8ByteSize which would have the same value as String.length and is still O(1)

Henrik Böving said:

You will still be able to count the unicode codepoints by just taking the length of the character iterator (though now in O(n) as opposed to O(1)).

Sounds like it's not a character iterator then?
Why not? docs#String.chars iterates over the code points in a string.
Exactly, code points are not characters
That codepoints correspond to the character type is normal, it's the case for Lean's Char, for Rust's char, for Haskell's Char etc.
You get what I mean though
I don't get what you mean. Are you saying that you would rather have an iterator over the grapheme clusters?

Edward van de Meent said:

Exactly, code points are not characters

Quoting the introduction of the Unicode standard:

The Unicode Standard specifies a numeric value (code point) and a name for each of
its characters.

So I would say that for all practical purposes, code points are characters.

Julia Markus Himmel said:

I don't get what you mean. Are you saying that you would rather have an iterator over the grapheme clusters?

I'm saying that that's what I would call a "character iterator".
I would call that a grapheme cluster iterator.
And we'd both be right as far as I'm concerned. I realise that this is getting off-topic though.

Either way, it is the case that s.length and s.chars.length always return the same result, as proved by combining docs#String.toList_chars, docs#Std.Iter.length_toList_eq_length, and docs#String.length_toList.
You'd be happy with Swift, where Character is indeed extended grapheme cluster: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/character
s.chars.length is presumably much less efficient at runtime than s.length, as it has to allocate all the char objects?

As you can see from the IR, no char objects are allocated:

/-
    def WellFounded.opaqueFix₃._at_.length.spec_0._redArg (x_1 : @& obj) (x_2 : @& obj) (x_3 : tobj) (x_4 : tobj) : tobj :=
      let x_5 : tobj := proj[1] x_1;
      let x_6 : tobj := proj[2] x_1;
      let x_7 : tobj := Nat.sub x_6 x_5;
      let x_8 : u8 := Nat.decEq x_3 x_7;
      dec x_7;
      case x_8 : u8 of
      Bool.false →
        let x_9 : tagged := String.Pos.next x_2 x_3 ◾;
        dec x_3;
        let x_10 : tagged := 1;
        let x_11 : tobj := Nat.add x_4 x_10;
        dec x_4;
        let x_12 : tobj := WellFounded.opaqueFix₃._at_.length.spec_0._redArg x_1 x_2 x_9 x_11;
        ret x_12
      Bool.true →
        dec x_3;
        ret x_4
-/
set_option trace.compiler.ir.result true in
def length (s : String) : Nat :=
  s.chars.length
(and char objects are not allocations anyways)
